newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia security chief pays first visit to Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Russia security chief pays first visit to Chechnya.

text.p: Russia's new security chief Ivan Rybkin headed for Chechnya on Sunday to pay his first visit to the breakaway region and talk to rebel leaders worried about the sacking of his predecessor Alexander Lebed.

Itar-Tass news agency said Rybkin had arrived in the neighbouring republic of Ingushetia from where he set off by car to the Chechen capital Grozny to meet the rebels as well as the commanders of Russian forces in the region.
In late August Lebed brokered a peace deal between Moscow and the separatists but the rebels say they are worried that his sacking could undermine the peace process.

Rybkin and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin have been at pains to reassure the separatists that Moscow does not want a return to violence. Tens of thousands of people were killed in the 21 months of war before the August 31 peace deal.

But conservative Kremlin officals and members of parliament oppose the deal, which called for the withdrawal of all Russian troops and said discussions on Chechnya's future status should be put on hold for five years.

After the deal, the rebels confirmed their plans to seek independence, took Chechnya under their control and unilaterally formed a "coalition government", defying an earlier agreement to cooperate with Russia in creating a post-war authority.

As Rybkin headed for Grozny, the 1,500-strong Congress of the Chechen People met to approve plans to hold local elections in January and to confirm the creation of separate posts of president and prime minister of Chechnya.
The congress last convened in 1990 when it declared the independence of the Chechen republic and laid the seeds for the present crisis.

The meeting opened in a Grozny building but delegates then moved to Urus-Martan, 35 km (20 miles) south-west of the Chechen capital, following a telephoned bomb warning, Tass said. An initial police search did not find any trace of a device.
Separatist leaders said on Saturday they opposed Moscow's plans to keep two brigades permanently in Chechnya.

The rebels, who saw the peace deal as a face-saving way for Moscow to let Chechnya go, insist all Russian troops should leave. Moscow has ruled out granting independence to Chechnya and the separatists fear hardliners could restart the war.
Russia's state security service chief Nikolai Kovalyov said on Wednesday the situation in Chechnya was a "serious danger" and warned of terrorism spreading across the country.

He said one of his priorities was to cooperate with the government and the Russian Security Council on stabilising the situation in Chechnya. But his warning of a terrorist threat appeared to cast doubt on the results of the Lebed peace deal.
